lesson.subtitle: Lesson 13 -- The Leadership Question
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flavio Gattaz | Lesson 13 -- The Leadership Question
lesson.grammar_point: emphasis and information order (fronting, negative-adverbial inversion, emphatic do)

listenings.text: I have sat on this committee for nine years, and the leadership question is the one candidates prepare the most and answer the worst. They come in with a story about a promotion, or a title, or a project that went well, and none of that is what I am listening for. I am listening for a moment when something was going wrong and a person decided. Not once in nine years have I given a high mark to a story with no cost in it. If the decision cost you nothing, you have told me about a task, and a task is not leadership. The second thing I listen for is what happened afterwards. A good answer has a ripple effect in it: the decision, and then the two or three things nobody planned that followed from it. And the third thing, which almost nobody does, is the order. Put the decision first and the context second. Candidates spend ninety seconds on the background and fifteen on what they actually did, and by then I have stopped counting.

The first time I answered the leadership question I told it in order, from the beginning, like a report. Two minutes on who the client was, who the engineer was and what the contract said, and then thirty seconds on the thing I actually did. The interviewer was polite and I could see her waiting. So the second time I started at the worst minute. I said: at six in the morning I stopped a pour with forty men on the site, and here is why. Everything else became background, and the background took forty seconds instead of two minutes. The other thing I changed was the ending. I used to finish with the result, because the result was good. Now I finish with what the decision set in motion, and I say the part that did not go well before anybody asks me for it. Nobody has second-guessed me since, and I think that is exactly why.
